passages.where: One gives freely and gains even more; another withholds and becomes poor; the one who refreshes others is refreshed. The site's note on the chapter says generosity that seems to lose ends up gaining, and hoarding that seems to gain ends up cursed. The proverb describes how God's world tends to work, not a scheme for profit.

Saying farewell to the Ephesian elders, Paul reminds them that he worked with his own hands to help the weak, remembering the Lord's words that it is more blessed to give than to receive. The site's plain note calls this Paul's last lesson, his own hands used for the weak, and asks whether you believe it, really, in your spending and your time. Giving is called a blessing before it is called a duty.

Paul tells of the Macedonian churches, who in deep poverty gave beyond their ability and begged to share in the gift for the believers in Jerusalem. The site's plain note says they gave themselves first to the Lord, and asks whether your money follows where your heart has already gone, or is the one thing you have kept back. It asks what would make giving feel like a privilege rather than a loss.

Paul grounds his appeal in Christ, who though rich became poor for their sake, so that through his poverty they might become rich. The site's plain note says the riches he gives are not money but forgiveness, a place in God's family, the Spirit and a future with God, and that Paul does not order the Corinthians to give but reminds them of Jesus. Christian generosity begins from what has already been given.

John asks how God's love can abide in anyone who sees a brother in need and closes his heart, and calls for love in action and truth. The site's plain note asks whom you know in need right now and whether your love costs you anything. It adds that this is love freely given, not letting someone take from you by force or fear.

Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and he will repay the lender. The site's note on the Hebrew word for lend says the borrower is elsewhere the weaker party, which makes the verse remarkable: God places himself in the borrower's position on behalf of the poor. A gift to the poor is never lost in God's accounts.

Jesus tells his followers to give so quietly that the left hand does not know what the right is doing, for the Father sees in secret. The site's note says he assumes they will give and attacks only the advertising of it, so that the poor are not turned into props for the giver's reputation. The plain note says the reward is not payment but the Father's notice of what no one else sees.

Israel is told not to reap to the edges of the field or strip the vineyard bare, but to leave the gleanings for the poor and the foreigner, ending with I am the LORD your God. The site's note on the chapter says every command is grounded in God's own character, with love of neighbour at the centre. Generosity was built into the way the harvest itself was done.

Jesus tells his host to invite the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind, who cannot repay. The site's note says the danger he names is not that the host will lose money but that he will be repaid, since generosity that expects a return is a transaction. The plain note says Jesus means real meals, and that a table which only ever holds people who can pay us back is too small.

In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, always occupied with works of kindness and charity, and the widows show the tunics she made for them. The site's plain note says she is remembered by what she made for others, and that small, faithful kindness is not small to God. Generosity in Acts is often a needle and thread.

misread.taken: Whoever sows generously will also reap generously is used to promise that money given to God, or to a particular ministry, will come back many times over.
misread.says: The site's plain note says no, plainly: Paul says God will give all that you need, not all that you want; the harvest he names is the harvest of your righteousness, goodness and not goods; and the riches are to be generous on every occasion, so that people thank God. The people in these chapters who give most freely are poor and stay poor, and the note on the chapter says the return on generosity is the capacity for more generosity, not personal wealth. If you gave because someone promised God would pay you back, the plain note says, that was not your failure; the promise was wrong.

whole: Most people want to be generous and find it harder than they expected. The bills come first, then the savings, then whatever is left, and there rarely is much left. Some give out of guilt or pressure and feel resentful afterwards. Some give and want it noticed. Some have been burned by appeals that promised a return or by charities that misused the gift, and have stopped giving at all. Others give money easily but not time, or time but not money. And some who have very little give more freely than those who have much, and do not think of it as anything special.

Scripture names what holds the hand closed. Proverbs sets the one who withholds beside the one who gives freely, and John asks how God's love can live in someone who sees a brother in need and shuts his heart. Jesus warns against giving to be seen, which turns the poor into props for a reputation, and against the generosity that is really a transaction, inviting only those who can invite you back. Beneath all of these lies fear, that there will not be enough, and the wish to stay in control of who owes what. Every one of us has felt the hand close at the wrong moment.

So the Bible's wisdom builds generosity into ordinary life. Israel left the edges of the field for the poor, so that giving was part of how the harvest was done. Paul told the Corinthians to give regularly and in proportion, and the Macedonians gave themselves first to the Lord and then their money. Jesus asks for quiet gifts the left hand does not know about, and for tables with guests who cannot repay. Tabitha's generosity was tunics, and Paul's was the work of his own hands for the weak. Give on purpose, cheerfully and not under pressure, and never because someone promised you a return.

The hope Scripture gives begins with a gift already made. Christ, though rich, became poor for our sake, and Paul does not order the Corinthians to give; he reminds them of Jesus. Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, who places himself in the borrower's seat. Those who refresh others are refreshed, not with a payout but with the joy Paul remembered in Jesus' words: it is more blessed to give than to receive.
sit: Who is in need near you right now, and what do you have that could help them this week?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says generosity in this psalm is part of what it means to fear the LORD, and asks whether what you have is open-handed, like seed scattered on a field. It adds that the psalm describes how God's world tends to work, not a promise of riches.
